newsitem.title: USA: Highlights of major tax cut provisions.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of major tax cut provisions.

text.p: The following are the highlights of the five-year plan to cut taxes by a net $95 billion -- the first major tax cut in 16 years:

CHILD TAX CREDIT - Provides a tax credit of $400 per child in 1998, $500 per child in 1999 and thereafter. The amount is deducted directly from income tax owed. It applies to children under age 17, and is available to families with adjusted gross income above $18,000. The credit starts to phase out at $75,000 for singles, $110,000 for couples.

Low income families with three or more children who pay little or no income taxes can take the credit against payroll taxes. The credit is in addition to earned income tax credits available for low-income families.

EDUCATION - Provides so-called Hope scholarship tax credits of up to $1,500 of tuition expenses for first two years of post-secondary education. It also provides a lifetime learning credit of up to 20 percent of tuition for a maximum $1,000 a year after the first two years of college. This 20 percent credit rises to maximum of $2,000 a year in 2003. The lifetime learning credits are available for any number of years of education. The credit can be taken by parents, spouses or the students themselves.

It also establishes education savings accounts of up to $500 per child that phase out at $150,000 of income for couples, $95,000 for singles. Parents may contribute up to $500 per child of after-tax income, but the earnings on the accounts are tax-free. The law allows tax-free withdrawals for higher education, and penalty-free withdrawals from retirement IRAs to pay for college. It also allows income tax deductions of up to $2,500 in interest on student loans each year for the first five years of repayment.
CAPITAL GAINS - The longer the asset is held, the lower the tax rate.

Effective July 29, the top capital gains tax rate is cut to 20 percent from 28 percent for assets held 18 months or longer. Assets held 12-18 months will be taxed at a maximum 28 percent rate. Assets held under one year will be taxed at the taxpayer's income tax rate, a maximum of 39.6 percent.
Assets held at least 12 months and sold between May 7-July 28, 1997, will be taxed at a maximum of 20 percent.
A new, lower long-term rate takes effect in 2001. Assets purchased after Dec. 30, 2000 and held at least five years will be taxed at a maximum 18 percent.

For taxpayers with income below $41,200, the maximum rate drops to 10 percent from 15 percent. They may take advantage of an 8 percent rate after Jan. 1, 2001 for assets held five years no matter when they were acquired.

RETIREMENT - Raises the income limits for so-called "front loaded" tax-deductible individual retirement accounts by $10,000 a year for couples and $5,000 for singles until maximum limit of $50,000 for singles and $80,000 for couples is reached in 2004.

Non-working spouses may save $2,000 a year regardless of their spouses' retirement plan in families with income under $150,000. A new non-deductible IRA starts Jan. 1, 1998 with maximum contribution of $2,000 a year. Income can be withdrawn tax free after retirement.
Investments in gold, silver and platinum bullion would be allowed in IRAs.

REAL ESTATE - Every two years a homeowner may exclude from taxable income all profits from the sale of a home up to $250,000 for an individual and up to $500,000 for a couple. it includes penalty-free withdrawal from IRA to help pay for a first home for the taxpayer, or a child or grandchild.
TOBACCO - The current 24 cents per pack cigarette tax rises to 34 cents in 2000 and 39 cents in 2002. Similar increase for other tobacco products.
AIRLINE TICKETS - Current ticket tax of 10 percent will be lowered to 7.5 percent over three years. International arrival and departure fee of $12 would be imposed on international flights.

ESTATE TAXES - Estates of family farms and small businesses may exclude $1.3 million of value in 1998 and beyond. Heirs must participate in the business for a decade after inheritance of the business or farm.
SELF-EMPLOYED - Deduction for health insurance made permanent and rise from 40 percent in 1997 to 100 percent by 2007.
